'''Ian Graeme Barbour''' (October 5, 1923 – December 24, 2013) was an American scholar on the [[relationship between science and religion]]. According to the [[Public Broadcasting Service]], his mid-1960s ''[[Issues in Science and Religion]]'' "has been credited with literally creating the contemporary field of science and religion."<ref name=PBS1>{{cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/forum/june99/barbour_bio.html |title=The PBS Online Newhour May 28, 1999 |website=[[PBS]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080122050215/https://www.pbs.org/newshour/forum/june99/barbour_bio.html |archive-date=January 22, 2008 |access-date=2008-06-30}}</ref>

In the citation nominating Barbour for the 1999 [[Templeton Prize]], [[John B. Cobb]] wrote, "No contemporary has made a more original, deep, and lasting contribution toward the needed integration of scientific and religious knowledge and values than Ian Barbour. With respect to the breadth of topics and fields brought into this integration, Barbour has no equal."<ref name="carleton.edu">{{cite web |date=March 10, 1999 |title=Carleton Professor Emeritus Wins Prestigious Templeton Prize |url=http://www.carleton.edu/campus/newsbureau/pr/barbour.html |location=Northfield, Minnesota |publisher=Carleton College |access-date=August 25, 2020}}</ref>

==Biography==
Barbour was born on October 5, 1923, in [[Beijing]], China,{{sfn|Russell|2014|p=123}}<ref name="Yardley 2014">{{cite news |last=Yardley |first=William |date=January 13, 2014 |title=Ian Barbour, Who Found a Balance Between Faith and Science, Dies at 90 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/01/13/us/ian-barbour-academic-who-resisted-conflicts-of-faith-and-science-dies-at-90.html |work=The New York Times |page=A19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140113042101/https://www.nytimes.com/2014/01/13/us/ian-barbour-academic-who-resisted-conflicts-of-faith-and-science-dies-at-90.html |archive-date=January 13, 2014 |access-date=August 24, 2020}}</ref> the second of three sons of an American [[Episcopalianism|Episcopal]] mother (who was the daughter of the [[obstetrician]] [[Robert Latou Dickinson]]) and a Scottish [[Presbyterian]] father.<ref name=PBS1/>{{sfn|Barbour|2017|p=5}} His family left China in 1931, and Barbour spent the remainder of his youth in the United States and England.{{sfnm |1a1=Barbour |1y=2017 |1p=5 |2a1=Russell |2y=2014 |2p=124}} A [[conscientious objector]], he served in the [[Civilian Public Service]] for three years during the [[Second World War]].{{sfn|Barbour|2017|p=6}}<ref name="Woo 2014">{{cite news |last=Woo |first=Elaine |date=January 1, 2014 |title=Ian Barbour Dies at 90; Academic Who Bridged Science–Religion Divide |url=http://www.latimes.com/obituaries/la-me-ian-barbour-20140102,0,4989882.story#axzz2qSCr5d8A |work=Los Angeles Times |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140121065637/http://articles.latimes.com/2014/jan/01/local/la-me-ian-barbour-20140102 |archive-date=January 21, 2014 |access-date=January 15, 2014}}</ref>

He received his [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[physics]] from [[Swarthmore College]] and his [[Master of Science]] degree in physics from [[Duke University]] in 1946.<ref name=PBS1/> In 1950, he received a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degree in physics from the [[University of Chicago]],<ref name=PBS1/> where he worked as a teaching assistant to [[Enrico Fermi]].<ref name=PBS1/>{{sfn|Barbour|2017|p=6}} He earned a [[Bachelor of Divinity]] degree in 1956 from [[Yale University's Divinity School]].<ref name=PBS1/>

Barbour taught at [[Carleton College]] beginning {{citation needed span |date=August 2020 |text=in 1955}} with a joint appointment in the departments of physics and philosophy.{{sfn|Barbour|2017|p=7}} He began teaching religion full-time in 1960, when the university established a religion department.{{sfn|Barbour|2017|p=7}} In the 1970s, he co-founded of the Science, Technology, and Public Policy program at Carleton, which later became the Environment and Technology Studies program.  He retired in 1986 as the Winifred and Atherton Bean Professor [[Emeritus]] of Science, Technology and Society.

Barbour gave the [[Gifford lectures]] from 1989 to 1991 at the [[University of Aberdeen]]. These lectures led to the book ''Religion in an Age of Science''.  He was awarded the [[Templeton Prize]] in 1999<ref name=PBS1/>{{sfn|Barbour|2017|p=9}} for Progress in Religion in recognition of his efforts to create a dialogue between the worlds of science and religion.

Barbour was married to Deane Kern from 1947 until her death in 2011.<ref name="Yardley 2014"/> They had four children.{{sfn|Russell|2014|p=124}}

Barbour suffered a stroke on December 20, 2013, at his home in [[Northfield, Minnesota|Northfield]], [[Minnesota]], and remained in a coma at [[Abbott Northwestern Hospital]] until his death four days later.<ref name="apps.carleton.edu">{{Cite web|url=http://apps.carleton.edu/farewells/?story_id=1081774|title = Ian Barbour - Carleton College}}</ref>

==Philosophy and theology==
In his efforts to link science and religion in ''[[Issues in Science and Religion]]'', Barbour coined the term ''[[Theological critical realism|critical realism]]''. This has been adopted by other scholars. He claimed the basic structure of religion is similar to that of science in some ways but also differs on some crucial points. They are part of the same spectrum in which both display subjective as well as objective features. The subjective includes the theory on data, the resistance of comprehensive theories to falsification, and the absence of rules for choice among paradigms. Objective features include the presence of common data, evidence for or against a theory, and criteria which are not paradigm-dependent. The presence of subjective and objective features in both science and religion makes his thinking valuable and original. Barbour's arguments have been developed in significant and diverse ways by a variety of scholars, including [[Arthur Peacocke]], [[John Polkinghorne]], [[Sallie McFague]], and [[Robert John Russell]]. His subjective/objective approach is prominent in the evolving paradigm of [[religious naturalism]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Russell |first=Robert John |author-link=Robert John Russell |title=Critical Realism: The Original Bridge Between Science and Religion |url=http://www.counterbalance.org/rjr/bcrit-body.html |location=Seattle, Washington |publisher=Counterbalance Foundation |access-date=15 April 2011}}</ref>

Barbour considered critical realism an alternative to the competing interpretations of scientific theories:  classical or naive realism, instrumentalism, and idealism. A critical realist perspective sees scientific theories yielding partial, revisable, abstract, but referential knowledge of the world that can be expressed through metaphors and models.

During the 1970s, Barbour presented a program of interdisciplinary courses that dealt with ethical issues in the applications of science, exploring the social and environmental consequences of a variety of technologies. In 2000, in ''When Science Meets Religion'' (2000) he used a fourfold typology (Conflict, Independence, Dialogue, Integration) to relate religion and science that he had developed in his earlier writings.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ian G. Barbour |url=http://www.giffordlectures.org/Author.asp?AuthorID=207 |website=Gifford Lectures |access-date=April 18, 2011 |archive-date=September 16, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110916033528/http://www.giffordlectures.org/Author.asp?AuthorID=207 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In his works, Barbour writes from a Christian perspective.<ref>{{cite web |last=Taylor |first=Howard |title=Review of ''When Science Meets Religion'', by Ian Barbour |url=http://www.hgtaylor.net/ian-barbour.htm |url-status=dead |website=Faith and the Modern World |publisher=Howard Taylor |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110521105703/http://www.hgtaylor.net/ian-barbour.htm |archive-date=2011-05-21 |access-date=2011-04-18}}</ref>{{self-published inline |date=August 2020 |certain=yes}}

Barbour compared methods of inquiry in science and religion, and has explored the theological implications of the [[natural science|natural]] and [[social science]]s. He also has lectured widely on ethical issues in such fields as [[climate change]], technology policy, energy, agriculture, computers, and [[cloning]].<ref name="carleton.edu"/>

American academic [[Forrest Clingerman]] ties Barbour to the religious naturalism movement via his theology of nature. His subjective/objective approach to religion is prominent in this evolving paradigm.{{sfn|Clingerman|2009|p=143}} [[Michael Dowd]] calls Barbour the grandfather of the evolutionary Christianity movement.<ref>[http://evolutionarychristianity.com/blog/general/ian-barbour-granddaddy-of-this-movement/ Grandddaddy of Evolutionary Christianity] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110210204142/http://evolutionarychristianity.com/blog/general/ian-barbour-granddaddy-of-this-movement/ |date=February 10, 2011}} retrieved April 15, 2011</ref>

In his acceptance speech for the 1999 [[Templeton Prize]], Barbour spoke about the need to break down barriers, using cloning as an example of science's ability to say what is possible and of religion to reflect on what is desirable.<ref name="Woo 2014"/>
